blocks.prompt: The Two Sponges in Your Chest
blocks.text: Your lungs are two soft, spongy bags inside your chest. When you breathe in, air rushes down a tube in your throat and fills them up. The air has something in it that your body needs. It is called oxygen. Your blood picks up the oxygen and carries it everywhere. Your toes need it. Your brain needs it. Then your lungs push out the air you are done with. Under your lungs is a flat muscle called the diaphragm. It pulls down to let air in. It pushes up to send air out. You breathe about 20,000 times a day. You almost never have to think about it.

blocks.prompt: The Tree Inside Your Chest
blocks.text: Take a deep breath. Air travels down your windpipe, a stiff tube in the front of your neck. At the bottom, the windpipe splits in two. One branch goes to your right lung. One goes to your left. Inside each lung, those branches split again, and again, and again, more than twenty times. The tubes get smaller every time, until they are thinner than a hair. Your lungs are shaped like an upside down tree. At the tip of every tiny branch hangs a bubble called an alveolus. You have about 300 million of them. Each bubble is wrapped in blood vessels so thin that oxygen can slip straight through the wall and into your blood. Carbon dioxide, the waste gas your body is finished with, slips the other way. Then you breathe out and it is gone. All those bubbles unfolded flat would cover half a tennis court. That whole surface is folded up inside your chest, and it fits.

blocks.prompt: The Muscle That Does the Breathing
blocks.text: Here is something strange about your lungs: they cannot move themselves. A lung has no muscle in it. It is a soft, springy sponge, and left alone it would simply sit there. The work of breathing is done by something else. Stretched across the bottom of your chest is a dome of muscle called the diaphragm. When it tightens, it flattens downward. At the same time, muscles between your ribs lift your rib cage up and out. Your chest gets bigger, and the air inside it spreads out to fill the extra room. That thins the air, and the thinner air presses less. Outside, the air of the whole sky is still pressing hard on you. So the outside air pushes in through your nose, down your windpipe, and into your lungs. You do not really suck air in. The atmosphere shoves it in, and you make the room for it. Breathing out is easier. Your diaphragm relaxes, your rib cage settles, and your stretched lungs spring back like a squeezed sponge letting go. Most of the time you never notice any of this. Your brain stem runs the rhythm without asking you, even while you sleep. But you can also grab the controls whenever you want: hold a breath, blow out a candle, sing a long note. Breathing is one of the very few jobs in your body that runs automatically and takes orders too.

blocks.prompt: The Alarm That Makes You Breathe
blocks.text: Try holding your breath. Within a minute, something in your chest begins to complain, then to shout. Most people assume that feeling is your body running out of oxygen. It is not. That alarm is triggered by carbon dioxide. Every cell you own burns oxygen to release energy, and every cell produces carbon dioxide as the leftover. The gas dissolves into your blood, where it turns the blood slightly acidic. Sensors in your brain stem and in your arteries are watching that acidity constantly. When it rises, they fire, and the urge to breathe arrives whether you like it or not. Your body monitors its waste far more closely than its fuel, because carbon dioxide builds up long before oxygen runs low. It is an early warning system, and it is why holding your breath is uncomfortable well before it is dangerous. It is also why you cannot hold your breath until you die. Push far enough and you lose consciousness. The moment you do, the brain stem takes back the controls it never really surrendered, and you breathe. Your body does not trust you with this job. The exchange itself happens in the alveoli, the hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs at the ends of your airways. The wall between the air and your blood there is astonishingly thin, less than a thousandth of a millimeter, far thinner than a sheet of paper. Oxygen crosses it and latches onto the red cells rushing past. Carbon dioxide crosses the other way. The air you breathe in is about 21 percent oxygen; the air you breathe out is still about 16 percent. You use surprisingly little of what you take, which is exactly why rescue breathing works. Your lungs also clean themselves. The airways are coated in sticky mucus, and beneath it stand millions of microscopic hairs called cilia, all beating upward in waves. Dust, pollen, and bacteria land in the mucus and get swept steadily up toward your throat, where you swallow them without noticing. Doctors call it the mucociliary escalator, and it runs day and night. One last oddity. Because of all that trapped air, healthy lungs are the only organs in your body that float in water. Coroners have used this fact for centuries to tell whether a newborn ever drew a breath.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The bronchial tree branches about 23 times
300 to 500 million alveoli
Surface area: roughly half a tennis court
Breathing is both automatic and voluntary
Air and food share one hallway, inherited from fish
Bird lungs move air in one direction only

blocks.prompt: The Only Organ You Can Command
blocks.text: Every other organ you own works in secret. You cannot order your liver to filter faster, or ask your kidneys to pause for thirty seconds. Your heart will not take requests. Your lungs are the exception. Breathing runs perfectly well without you, and yet you can seize the controls at any moment, hold a breath underwater, blow out a match, shape a sentence. That double life is not an accident. It is the reason the lungs are one of the strangest pieces of engineering in the body. Start with the machine itself. A lung contains no muscle. It is a passive sponge, and it does nothing on its own. Breathing is performed by the diaphragm, a dome of muscle slung under the chest, working with the muscles laced between your ribs. When they contract, the chest cavity enlarges. The air already inside spreads out, its pressure drops below the pressure of the atmosphere outside, and the outside air rushes in to even the score. You never pull air into your body. You enlarge a space, and the sky fills it. Where that air ends up is the real marvel. Your windpipe divides into two bronchi, one per lung, and each of those divides, and divides again, roughly twenty-three times over, branching into a tree of tubes finer than hairs. At the very tips hang the alveoli, between 300 and 500 million air sacs, each wrapped in capillaries. The barrier separating air from blood there is thinner than a thousandth of a millimeter. Oxygen drifts across it and binds to hemoglobin in the red cells streaming past; carbon dioxide drifts back the other way. Spread flat, all that folded surface would cover roughly half a tennis court. Your body carries a tennis court around inside a chest the size of a school bag. Every advantage here is also a cost. A surface large enough and thin enough for gases to cross is, by definition, a surface thin enough for almost anything else to cross. Your lungs are the widest open door in your body, and you hold it open twenty thousand times a day, admitting dust, smoke, pollen, viruses, and spores with every breath. So the lungs are defended obsessively. Mucus lines the airways to trap intruders. Beneath it, carpets of microscopic hairs called cilia beat upward in coordinated waves, walking the mucus toward your throat to be swallowed. Immune cells patrol the sacs themselves. Nearly every serious lung disease is a story about that defense failing or overreacting: smoke that paralyzes the cilia, an infection that floods the sacs with fluid, an immune system that clamps the airways shut at the sight of a cat. Even the layout is a compromise. Air and food share a single hallway at the back of your throat, an arrangement inherited from fish and never redesigned, which is why a swallow at the wrong moment can kill you. Birds, meanwhile, ended up with a better lung than ours: air flows through it in one direction, fresh in every phase of the cycle, which is part of how a goose crosses the Himalayas in air that would leave you unconscious. Your lungs are not the finest breathing machine on the planet. They are a very old design, patched and compromised, running on borrowed anatomy. They are also good enough that you have never once had to remember to use them.
